facts.claim_en: Nodake is one of Aogashima's two documented seasonal wild bamboo shoots and may be grilled and peeled before eating.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: A second slender bamboo shoot follows nodake in the island's seasonal gathering calendar.

facts.claim_en: Nigadake appears after nodake and is a somewhat bitter bamboo shoot used in simmered foods.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: Wild yams are dug from the ground in autumn; their aerial bulbils also form a separate household food tradition.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima residents traditionally dig wild yams after the above-ground growth dies back in autumn.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: A local rice preparation uses the small aerial bulbils produced by wild yams.

facts.claim_en: The island calls wild-yam bulbils kango and uses them in kango rice.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: Small wild grape-like fruits are used as a sour flavoring, including with freshly caught fish.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima fishermen have used sour ebezu fruit to season freshly caught fish.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: An island citrus known locally as kabutsu supplies acidity to seafood, hot-pot sauces and shochu.

facts.claim_en: Kabutsu is Aogashima's local name for a daidai citrus traditionally gathered and used as a sour seasoning.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: Wild ashitaba is a staple island green, eaten blanched, seasoned or stir-fried.

facts.claim_en: Ashitaba grows across Aogashima and is an important ingredient in local household cooking.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: Despite its name, kujirayo refers to a fish, not a whale. It is eaten grilled, raw or pickled.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's kujirayo is the fish known as tenjiku-isaki and is a representative local seafood.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.season_en: Caught year-round; the village also associates winter with particularly good fish.
food_cultures.notes_en: The local name must not be interpreted as whale meat.

food_cultures.summary_en: The island gathers seaweed from coastal rocks when the winter sea permits and uses it in rice and hot-pot dishes.

facts.claim_en: Rock seaweed is harvested around Aogashima's coast and used in nori rice and seaweed hot pots.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: This broad seaweed is gathered in winter and cooked with rice or incorporated into fritters with ashitaba.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's hamba seaweed is used in hamba rice and fritters with ashitaba.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: A reddish-purple seaweed associated with winter seafood and used in clear soups.

facts.claim_en: Shibousaki is a locally gathered reddish seaweed used in Aogashima soups.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: Locally collected shellfish are used in rice dishes, miso soup and preserved preparations.

facts.claim_en: The island collects hirami shellfish and prepares them in rice, soup and salted dishes.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.season_en: Year-round; collection can be easier around May.

food_cultures.summary_en: A coastal crustacean gathered from rocks and prepared in miso soup or steamed with sake.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima calls goose barnacles senokami and eats them in soup or sake-steamed preparations.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: A slender local moray eel is dried for simmering or prepared fresh as tempura.

facts.claim_en: Kanbeeme is a slender moray eel eaten dried and simmered, or cut and fried when fresh.
facts.source_title: 特産品 -野菜やお芋、魚や貝たち-

food_cultures.summary_en: The island's own version of Izu Islands sushi places soy-marinated fish over rice dressed with mustard.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's island sushi uses mustard and soy-marinated local seafood, including several types of sea bream and other fish.

food_cultures.notes_en: The village documents it as traditional food, but this source does not identify a specific public dining venue.

food_cultures.summary_en: A celebratory sweet-savory chicken hot pot seasoned with soy sauce and sugar, with ashitaba added to balance its richness.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's traditional torinabe uses chicken extensively, combines it with ashitaba and is commonly finished with noodles.

food_cultures.notes_en: The village identifies it as one of the island's familiar celebratory dishes.

food_cultures.summary_en: A winter dish featuring local red grouper cooked in miso soup.

facts.claim_en: Akaba miso soup is a characteristic winter preparation on Aogashima.

food_cultures.summary_en: A household soup combining local sweet potatoes and ashitaba.

facts.claim_en: Kanmo-jiru is a local soup made with sweet potatoes, ashitaba and other ingredients.

food_cultures.summary_en: A related island soup substitutes taro for sweet potato.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's imo-jiru uses taro in place of the sweet potatoes found in kanmo-jiru.

food_cultures.summary_en: Sweet potatoes are sliced and dried as a traditional preserved food.

facts.claim_en: Kinboshi is made by slicing and drying kanmo sweet potatoes.

food_cultures.summary_en: An intensely flavored preserved seafood preparation using salted fish parts, including bones and scraps.

facts.claim_en: Shuude is a strongly flavored salted seafood preparation that makes use of fish scraps.

food_cultures.summary_en: A simple traditional preparation of locally grown island cucumber rubbed with salt.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima lists salted and massaged island cucumber as a local dish.

food_cultures.season_en: The cucumber crop is associated with June–September.

food_cultures.name_en: Pounded taro, sweet potato and ashitaba
food_cultures.summary_en: A rustic dish of boiled local roots and greens pounded together.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's imotsuki combines boiled taro, sweet potato and ashitaba, which are then pounded.

food_cultures.summary_en: A traditional preparation combining cooked, flaked fish with daikon and its leaves.

facts.claim_en: Iritori mixes cooked fish flesh with daikon radish and daikon greens.

food_cultures.name_en: Minced flying fish and vegetable salad
food_cultures.summary_en: A local seafood preparation combines chopped flying fish with vegetables and seasonal wild plants.

facts.claim_en: Bota-ae is made with chopped flying fish and ingredients including daikon and itadori.

food_cultures.summary_en: A substantial barley porridge cooked with local vegetables and miso.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's barley porridge includes burdock, ashitaba and taro, and is seasoned with miso.

food_cultures.summary_en: A local way of preparing fish such as kujirayo by salting and pickling in vinegar.

facts.claim_en: Aogashima's suzuke uses salted fish, including kujirayo, preserved or seasoned with vinegar.

food_cultures.summary_en: Locally harvested rock seaweed is incorporated into an omelet, linking coastal gathering with household cuisine.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo Islands tourism information identifies rock-seaweed omelet among Aogashima's local foods.
facts.publisher: 東京都島しょ振興公社

food_cultures.summary_en: Marine foods from the surrounding waters include tuna, flying fish and medai, supplying island seafood traditions.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo's fisheries federation lists tuna, flying fish and medai among the fish caught around Aogashima.
facts.publisher: 東京都漁業協同組合連合会

places.address_ja: 東京都青ヶ島村

food_cultures.notes_en: The harbor is a cultural landscape, not a documented public fish-tasting venue.

food_cultures.summary_en: A local sushi tradition featuring marinated white fish such as sawara, sweetened rice and mustard in place of wasabi.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara island sushi uses soy-and-mirin-marinated local white fish, with mustard as its characteristic condiment.

food_cultures.summary_en: A characteristic island soup prepared using locally caught red grouper.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara's tourism association identifies miso soup made with local akaba grouper as a regional specialty.

food_cultures.summary_en: Local chili is crushed into soy sauce as a pungent alternative to wasabi when eating fresh fish.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara residents season sashimi by crushing locally grown hot chili into soy sauce.

food_cultures.name_en: Sea turtle stew and traditional turtle dishes
food_cultures.summary_en: Green sea turtle has a documented place in Ogasawara food history, especially in stews. Chichijima and Hahajima have different traditional seasonings.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara turtle stew is traditionally associated with a salt-based preparation on Chichijima and a soy-based preparation on Hahajima.

food_cultures.summary_en: A traditional fish preparation with roots attributed to Hawaii, using fish, vegetables and sour citrus or vinegar.

facts.claim_en: Tokyo Metropolitan Government describes pimaka as an Ogasawara home dish of fish and daikon marinated with vinegar and daidai juice, with possible Hawaiian roots.

food_cultures.notes_en: An important example of Ogasawara's Pacific cultural connections.

food_cultures.summary_en: A Western-influenced island soup made with chicken broth, vegetables and flour dumplings.

facts.claim_en: Dumplen is an Ogasawara home-cooking tradition believed to have been introduced by nineteenth-century American settlers.

food_cultures.notes_en: Distinctive for its connection to the islands' early multilingual settlement history.

food_cultures.summary_en: One of the islands' signature subtropical crops, consumed fresh or processed into drinks, jams and confectionery.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara mainly grows the Tainong No. 1 passion fruit cultivar and uses the harvest in fresh and processed products.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara's island mini tomatoes are grown locally and are known for their high sweetness.

facts.claim_en: The island's Kikuchi lemon was introduced after World War II through Hachijojima from Tinian and is usually harvested while its skin remains green.

food_cultures.summary_en: A traditional local drink pairs diluted shochu with aromatic island lemon.

facts.claim_en: Mizu-lemon, made by adding local island lemon to diluted shochu, is a long-standing favorite in Ogasawara.

food_cultures.summary_en: One of Japan's historically significant coffee-growing traditions began with settlers who arrived in 1830. Historic Typica coffee plants remain part of contemporary island cultivation.

facts.claim_en: Coffee plants arrived with Ogasawara's early settlers in 1830, and the islands continue to cultivate coffee including Typica plants descended from historical introductions.

food_cultures.notes_en: The existence of a historic place named Coffee Mountain does not establish visitor access to a particular plantation.

food_cultures.summary_en: Local beekeeping produces honey from flowers in the islands' subtropical environment.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara's warm climate allows honeybees to remain active through winter, and local honey is a recognized island product.

food_cultures.season_en: Principal harvests in June and November.

food_cultures.summary_en: Large pomelos have a long island history and are referenced in traditional Ogasawara song.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara cultivates different pomelo types, and the fruit is mentioned in the local folk song Marukibune.

food_cultures.summary_en: A historically important citrus associated with nineteenth-century settlement and the visit of Commodore Perry.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara oranges were observed by members of Perry's expedition during their 1853 visit, and surviving island trees remain a subject of agricultural study.

food_cultures.summary_en: Local banana cultivation includes King, Sanshaku and Sankaku varieties, reflecting the islands' long subtropical agricultural history.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara cultivates King, Sanshaku and Sankaku bananas; the King variety is associated with a long island-growing tradition.

food_cultures.summary_en: The islands' subtropical conditions and protected growing facilities support commercially significant Japanese-grown cacao.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara is associated with Japan's first large-scale commercial cacao cultivation, beginning in 2010.

makers.relation_en: Confectionery company associated with cultivating and using Ogasawara cacao.

food_cultures.summary_en: A chocolate brand built around cacao cultivated in Tokyo's Ogasawara Islands.

food_cultures.notes_en: The chocolate's island-grown raw material should not be confused with an assertion that the finished chocolate is manufactured on Ogasawara.

food_cultures.summary_en: Vanilla is cultivated locally and processed into island specialty products.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows vanilla and processes the harvested crop for food products.

food_cultures.summary_en: Island mango growing has a long history, with older trees surviving from before World War II.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows mangoes, particularly the Irwin variety, and still has surviving trees planted before the war.

food_cultures.name_ja: パパイヤ・青パパイヤ
food_cultures.summary_en: The island uses ripe papaya as fruit and unripe green papaya as a vegetable.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows papaya year-round, eating ripe fruits fresh and preparing unripe fruits as vegetables.

food_cultures.summary_en: A colorful cactus fruit cultivated on Ogasawara, with white- and red-fleshed types.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara cultivates dragon fruit, including different flesh-color varieties eaten fresh or frozen.

food_cultures.name_ja: スターフルーツ（ゴレンシ）
food_cultures.summary_en: This unusual star-shaped fruit is cultivated locally and has more than one harvesting period.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows starfruit, also called gorenshi, and harvests it in separate seasonal windows.

food_cultures.summary_en: A locally grown custard-like fruit from the Annona family.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara cultivates shakatou, an Annona fruit eaten fresh or made into drinks and frozen desserts.

food_cultures.summary_en: Another locally cultivated sweet Annona-family fruit.

facts.claim_en: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government identifies atemoya among Ogasawara's cultivated subtropical fruits.

food_cultures.summary_en: A sweet subtropical fruit cultivated as part of the islands' diversity of Annona-family crops.

facts.claim_en: Cherimoya is identified as a cultivated Ogasawara fruit.

food_cultures.name_ja: シャシャップ（トゲバンレイシ）
food_cultures.summary_en: A locally grown Annona-family fruit with more acidity than the island's other custard-apple relatives.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows shashappu, or soursop, which has a distinctive acidic flavor.

food_cultures.name_ja: イオウトウトウガラシ
food_cultures.summary_en: A particularly hot chili with roots on Iwo-to, later introduced to Chichijima and Hahajima.

facts.claim_en: Iwo-to chili was brought from Iwo-to to Chichijima and Hahajima after World War II and is used to season sashimi.

food_cultures.summary_en: A winged-pod vegetable introduced to help supply fresh vegetables during the islands' warm season.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara cultivates winged beans, especially the Urizun cultivar, and eats the pods in tempura, dressed dishes and other preparations.

food_cultures.summary_en: The Ogasawara Islands grow a round-podded okra variety introduced from Hachijojima.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara's Hachijo-type okra has tender round pods and originated from a variety introduced from Hachijojima.

food_cultures.summary_en: Potatoes grown in the islands' red soils form part of their distinctive seasonal vegetable production.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara grows potatoes in red island soil, including Danshaku, Kitaakari, May Queen and Dejima cultivars.

food_cultures.summary_en: An older island taro crop whose edible roots and leaf stalks have been used since before World War II.

facts.claim_en: Mizuimo has been eaten on Ogasawara since before the war, using both its tubers and edible stalks.

food_cultures.summary_en: Rum connects the islands' sugarcane cultivation with their nineteenth-century settlement history and later revival of local distilling.

facts.claim_en: Ogasawara's rum tradition grew out of sugarcane cultivation and earlier local spirits called awazake or mitsuzake; the modern rum company was established in 1989.
